bottom_line: Tech and AI stocks just had their worst week since 2020, and at the same time the Fed (the people who set interest rates) looks ready to raise rates again in December because inflation won't go away. Falling stocks plus pricier borrowing is the squeeze to watch right now.

stories.title: AI stocks had a brutal week
stories.real: Tech had its worst week on Wall Street since 2020, and Nvidia's stock had its longest weekly losing streak since 2008. Anthropic, a big AI company, made its record debut on the Nasdaq stock market the same week, right into the selling.

stories.title: Fed likely raising rates again
stories.real: The Fed's own meeting notes say higher rates are needed in December because worries about inflation are growing. Traders now put the odds of a December hike at over 90%. President Trump says rates are too high and calls the Fed 'politicized', and Fed Chair Kevin Warsh is caught in the middle.
stories.you: If the Fed raises rates, credit cards, car loans and other borrowing usually get more expensive, and savings accounts usually pay a bit more.

stories.title: Inflation still the big problem
stories.real: New inflation numbers come out this week, and some watchers see 'really bad signs' ahead of them. So far, US shoppers are still spending going into the holidays.
stories.you: Prices rising faster than expected is the main reason the Fed wants to raise rates, so this report matters for your loan costs.

stories.title: Push to cap credit card rates
stories.real: Trump says he will work with Democrats to cap credit card interest rates at 10%. It is a promise for now, not a law.
stories.you: If it ever passed, people who carry a credit card balance would pay less interest. Nothing changes until Congress acts.

stories.title: Jobs cooling a little
stories.real: Slightly more Americans applied for unemployment help, but the number is still low compared with history. In Australia, the jobless rate rose to its highest level since 2021.
stories.you: The US job market is still holding up overall, but it is worth keeping an emergency fund in case hiring slows.
